quote: Klassenanzahl 1 ein Körper mit höherer Klassenanzahl entstehen kann.
english: ...class number 1 a field with higher class number can arise.
topic: Research notes listing three tasks: determining class numbers of multiquadratic fields (especially biquadratic fields), defining the lemniscate function by algebraic approximation following a hint by Gauss, and finding all quartic equations with rational coefficients and discriminant ±1.

triage.modern_statement: The fragment is cut off, so this is a reconstruction. It probably asks: if K1 and K2 are number fields with class number 1 (most likely quadratic fields, given the page's topic of multiquadratic and biquadratic fields), can their compositum K1K2 (e.g. a biquadratic field Q(√a,√b)) have class number h > 1? In modern terms this is a question about how h(K1K2) relates to h(K1) and h(K2). For biquadratic fields, Kuroda's class number formula answers it: h(K) = Q(K)·h1·h2·h3/2 for imaginary K and /4 for real K (when the base field is Q). Here h1, h2, h3 are the class numbers of the three quadratic subfields and Q(K) is the unit index. The third quadratic subfield Q(√ab) can have class number greater than 1 even when h(Q(√a)) = h(Q(√b)) = 1.
triage.answered_by: Dirichlet already knew the special case Q(√−1, √m), giving h_K in terms of h2·h3 and a unit index. Later Bachmann, Amberg and Herglotz (around 1922) worked on it, followed by Kuroda's general class number formula (1950) and Kubota's work on biquadratic fields (1956). Lemmermeyer has since given a non-analytic proof of Kuroda's formula. The worked example is my own calculation with standard class numbers, not taken from a source: h(Q(√2)) = h(Q(√−7)) = 1 but h(Q(√−14)) = 4, so the formula gives h(Q(√2,√−7)) ∈ {2, 4}, which is greater than 1. So the answer is yes. I found no source that refers to this diary entry itself.

evidence.claim: Kuroda's formula relates the class number of a multiquadratic number field to the class numbers of its quadratic subfields, with the unit group index as a key component.
Dirichlet already knew a formula for Q(√−1, √m) expressing h_K through q(K)·h2·h3. Bachmann, Amberg and Herglotz did later work, and Hasse gave a formula in the 1950s.
Lemmermeyer gives a non-analytic proof of the class number formula for biquadratic extensions of number fields.
There is an elementary formulation of Kubota's proof of Satz 4 about biquadratic number fields.

Proposition 1.5 there concerns the class number of the compositum E of two number fields F and K with relatively prime discriminants. This shows that the class numbers of composita are studied in their own right.

triage.why: The text is a fragment, and the subject of 'can arise' (presumably a compositum or multiquadratic field built from fields with class number 1) is my reconstruction from the page topic. If that reading is right, the question was settled. Dirichlet's case and Kuroda's formula (1950) give the class number of a biquadratic field in terms of its three quadratic subfields. The third subfield can have a larger class number, so the compositum can too; the Q(√2,√−7) example is my own check, not from a source. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Kuroda's formula and the class numbers of multiquadratic fields are still studied today (e.g. the 2021 Math. Z. paper on arithmetic statistics). Confidence is low because I can't be sure what the fragment refers to.
